text: Bramwell Logistics' detection-to-containment script from Lesson 29 now lives in a real git repository with pull requests and a path to production -- exactly the kind of repository Chapter 7 warned shouldn't ship without its own protections. This lab adds a real security gate to that pipeline, built from the tools Chapter 6 covered.

The workflow adds a dependency scan with pip-audit and a static-analysis scan with bandit against the script's own source. Both steps use continue-on-error, deliberately, because pip-audit exits non-zero on any finding at all, including a single Low-severity one -- and the gate script, not the scanner's raw exit code, needs to make the real pass or fail decision.

One small Python script reads both scanners' JSON reports and counts only the Critical and High severity findings as build-blocking. Trusting each tool's own exit code would mean maintaining two separate, inconsistent thresholds. One gate script making one deliberate decision keeps that threshold policy in exactly one place.

That Critical-and-High-only threshold is a direct application of Lesson 24's argument: a gate that fails the build on every Low and Medium finding trains a team to ignore it within a week. Everything below the threshold still shows up in the uploaded report for a reviewer to see -- it just doesn't block the merge.

The gate script gets wired into the workflow as its own step, and the scan reports upload with if: always, so they're attached to the run even when the gate step fails and stops the job -- no reviewer has to re-run the scan locally just to see what blocked them.

The real proof this gate works isn't reading its code -- it's watching it fail. A pull request that pins a dependency with a known Critical vulnerability has to turn the required check red, and reverting that pin has to turn it green again. Lesson 31 looks at what happens when a different automation script skips exactly this kind of deliberate guardrail.
